extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, legal advisors, and scholars concerned with state succession, treaty continuity, and international trade law in the Canada–Québec context
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/policy guidance on how treaties, GATT membership, and economic-integration arrangements are treated when a territory (Québec) becomes sovereign; assesses criteria for treaty continuity, accession/succession to international agreements, and elements defining the Canadian economic space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 34 Vienna Convention — succession in case of separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 34. Succession d’Etats en cas de séparation de parties d'un Etat — 'Lorsqu’une partie ou des parties du territoire d'un Etat se séparent pour former un ou plusieurs Etats... tout traité en vigueur en date de la succession d’Etats à l'égard de l'ensemble du territoire de l'Etat prédécesseur reste en vigueur à l'égard de chaque Etat successeur ainsi formé; ...' (with further subparagraphs on treaties applying only to part of territory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the baseline rule that treaties in force at the date of succession remain in force vis‑à‑vis successor states, subject to the exceptions listed in the article (agreement otherwise; incompatibility with object and purpose; radical change in execution conditions). The page uses this article to test whether Québec would automatically succeed to the Canada–US FTA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to automatic treaty continuity (Article 34 exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paragraph 1 exceptions: (a) if the States concerned agree otherwise; (b) if it appears from the treaty or is established otherwise that application of the treaty to the successor State would be incompatible with the object and purpose of the treaty or would radically change the conditions of its execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions are the legal tests to determine whether a successor state must be bound by a predecessor's treaty. The text applies them to argue that introducing a third partner into an originally bilateral treaty 'changerait radicalement les conditions d’exécution du traité', thus excluding succession of full operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bilateral-to-trilateral change as ground against automatic succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of a third partner into an agreement originally conceived as bilateral changes radically, by force of things, the conditions of execution of the treaty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report argues that adding the Québec as a third party to the Canada–US FTA would sufficiently change institutional arrangements (binational commissions, dispute settlement groups, working groups) so as to prevent automatic succession; therefore, succession would be plausible only after agreement by Canada and the US on necessary modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: De facto application pending agreement (practical interim approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending an agreement to modify the treaty, 'une application de facto des dispositions de fond de l'Accord pourrait être envisagée, à l'instar de ce qui se fait fréquemment au GATT dans de pareils cas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical interim application of substantive provisions can be envisaged while formal arrangements are negotiated, following GATT practice — i.e., functional continuity may be preserved de facto before formal succession or accession is completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to present new arrangements to GATT Parties (Article XXIV considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any new arrangement (e.g., Québec–Canada–US arrangement) should be submitted to the Contracting Parties of GATT as envisaged in Article XXIV of the General Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past practice: accession and association agreements (e.g., post‑entry-in‑force accessions to the Treaty of Rome, EFTA associations) have been presented to GATT Parties. The new arrangement must demonstrate compliance with Article XXIV requirements, notably extension of the agreement to 'l'essentiel des échanges' between the members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article XXIV GATT — criteria for free-trade agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Article XXIV allows signature of bilateral/multilateral free-trade agreements (more liberal regimes) but requires that such agreements meet Article XXIV conditions, including coverage of substantially all trade between the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Québec sought to join an existing FTA under Article XXIV, it would need to show the accession/extension meets Article XXIV's quantitative and substantive coverage tests — the page highlights the need to show the agreement extends to the essential part of trade between Québec and partners.

rubrics_metrics.name: GATT accession routes: negotiation (Article XXXIII) vs succession (Article XXVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two ways for new State accession to GATT: (1) accession by negotiation (Article XXXIII) — the regular route; (2) accession by succession (Article XXVI) — when a territory acquires full autonomy in external commercial relations, allowing it to be reputed signatory retroactively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The succession procedure has in practice supplanted the negotiated accession route for territories achieving autonomy; succession presumes adoption of the predecessor State's concessions and tariff schedule at date of accession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of accession by succession under GATT
rubrics_metrics.description: A territory that gains full autonomy in external commercial relations is deemed a signatory of the Agreement; other signatories must admit the new State as successor retroactively to the date of sovereignty; the new State is presumed to accept without restrictions the conditions and requirements applicable to the predecessor State (i.e., takes on the predecessor's tariff schedule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: Québec becoming a GATT member by succession would adopt the Canadian tariff schedule in force at accession date; the page emphasizes this presumption of continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to demonstrate compliance with Article XXIV for FTA accession
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the Canada–US FTA were to be approved for Québec, it would be necessary to appear before GATT to demonstrate that Québec's adhesion also meets Article XXIV requirements, particularly regarding extension to the bulk of trade between Québec and partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past practice requires presentation to Contracting Parties and demonstration of substantive coverage; the text cites prior accession/association precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: US political-practical reaction test — stability preference
rubrics_metrics.description: US, for political reasons, will favor any solution that prevents instability and conflict in Canada; thus it is unlikely to refuse to negotiate with Québec or to impose excessively onerous conditions purely to exclude Québec.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion assesses likely US behavior: preference for arrangements preserving economic union and avoiding destabilization, making outright refusal to negotiate or punitive conditions improbable.

rubrics_metrics.name: US economic-interest test (energy and market access considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: US economic interests (notably guaranteed access to Canadian energy resources, including Quebec hydroelectricity) make it unlikely that the US would forgo gains secured in the FTA or refuse to negotiate with Québec.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report argues it would be surprising for the US to relinquish access to hydroelectric resources or other FTA benefits; ongoing US negotiations with Mexico and Latin America make exclusion of Québec unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of accession to press bilateral grievances is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: The US might be tempted to use Québec's accession request to settle disputes (e.g., alcohol trade, supply-management issues), but because these problems also exist with the rest of Canada, imposing special conditions on Québec would amount to partial renegotiation of the Agreement and is unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical/political constraints: treating Québec differently on issues that affect all of Canada would be difficult and dangerous, and many such issues are already subject to GATT discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Canadian economic space — four freedoms and institutional harmonization
rubrics_metrics.description: The Canadian economic space is characterized by near-complete freedom of movement of persons, goods, services, and capital; it functions as more than a free-trade area — a customs union, monetary union, and de facto common market with uniform regulatory frameworks in key areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements supporting this characterization include the Charter right to mobility, absence of interprovincial tariffs (Const. s.121), federal jurisdiction over external trade and money, harmonized fiscal regimes, and sectoral regulatory uniformity (banking, telecommunications, IP, weights/measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for free movement of persons (mobility safeguards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Canadian Charter rights grant citizens/residents the right to establish and earn a living in any province, subject only to general laws that do not discriminate primarily on residence; transferability of social program rights and portability of pension assets facilitate interprovincial mobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These legal and administrative instruments constitute the measure of personal mobility within Canada and are contrasted with what might be lost under sovereignty scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for free movement of goods (constitutional and regulatory bases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Free circulation of goods is ensured by the absence of interprovincial tariffs (Const. s.121) and the federal competence over external commercial policy; provinces may enact indirect barriers (product standards, procurement policies, provincial monopolies), but harmonization and federal oversight limit their effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples of remaining barriers include provincial liquor corporation pricing and local production requirements; supply-management marketing boards (quotas) are identified as potential interprovincial impediments and sources of Québec advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for free movement of services and capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Services generally circulate freely across provinces, with exceptions for regulated professions and certain financial services; federal competence over telecommunications, navigation, air and rail transport, and banking ensures sectoral uniformity; a common currency and national banking system facilitate capital mobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmonization efforts (e.g., provincial regulation harmonization for transport, securities commissions cooperation) reduce interprovincial barriers; use of a single currency minimizes transaction costs and exchange risk between jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal and tax harmonization as an integration criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial harmonization of federal and provincial tax regimes — e.g., corporate tax collection agreements, uniform formulas for allocation of taxable income, and harmonization of provincial sales taxes with federal GST/TPS — is a key element of the economic union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites concrete mechanisms (provincial–federal collection agreements, perception arrangements, harmonization of TPS with Quebec sales tax) that preserve economic integration and reduce costs of fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of economic space as policy objective (efficiency and avoidance of fragmentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining the essential elements of the Canadian economic space is important because it allows better resource allocation and minimizes unproductive costs associated with market fragmentation; a code of conduct could state principles and acceptable practices and provide enforcement mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission considered but did not recommend constitutional entrenchment of such a code, reasoning that the economic union functions generally well and restrictions on interprovincial trade are not quantitatively large enough to justify deep constitutional reform.
